lesson.title: Places with several measures
lesson.text: When features are places, each paragraph may describe several measures and several results. Statements pick out one of them. Don't stop reading a paragraph after finding one match, because the same place may answer two or three statements.

questions.q: Excessive extraction of underground water has caused the land to subside.
questions.evidence: water has been extracted faster than it is replaced, the ground has been sinking.

questions.q: It reuses a greater proportion of treated wastewater than any other country.
questions.evidence: reuses most of it for agriculture – a far higher share than in any other country.

questions.q: Payments encouraged people to change the plants in their gardens.
questions.evidence: offered payments to residents who replaced water-intensive lawns with plants suited to dry conditions.

questions.q: A crisis was avoided partly because of a change in the weather.
questions.evidence: Day Zero was avoided, helped by the eventual return of rain.
questions.explanation: "Return of rain" = "a change in the weather".

questions.q: Public information was used to persuade people to accept a new source of water.
questions.evidence: Public education campaigns were used to overcome initial reluctance to drink recycled water.

questions.q: A great deal of water is lost through damaged infrastructure.
questions.evidence: leaks from damaged pipes waste a large proportion of the city's water.

questions.q: A particular method of watering crops was pioneered there.
questions.evidence: Its farmers helped pioneer drip irrigation.

questions.q: It has aimed to reduce its reliance on water supplied by another country.
questions.evidence: To reduce this dependence [on water imported from Malaysia].

lesson.title: Evidence attached to the right hypothesis
lesson.text: When a passage presents several hypotheses, each with its own evidence, statements often describe a piece of evidence rather than the hypothesis itself. Ask: "Which hypothesis is this evidence used to support or challenge?" Some evidence is used by two camps in different ways, so check the direction in the specific sentence.

questions.q: Evidence from a metal rarely found in the Earth's crust supported it.
questions.evidence: high concentrations of iridium, a metal that is rare in the Earth's crust.
questions.explanation: The iridium evidence supports the impact hypothesis.

questions.q: Its supporting evidence may have been partly caused by an incomplete fossil record.
questions.evidence: this apparent decline might partly reflect gaps in the fossil record.
questions.explanation: This is evidence for gradual decline, and it was questioned.

questions.q: It suggests that one event may have intensified another.
questions.evidence: others suggest that the impact may even have intensified the eruptions.
questions.explanation: This appears in the paragraph on combined explanations and involves both events.

questions.q: A geological feature discovered in the 1990s was seen as confirming it.
questions.evidence: identified a buried crater ... For many scientists, the discovery confirmed the Alvarez hypothesis.

questions.q: Supporters claim its contribution has not been sufficiently recognised.
questions.evidence: arguing that ... their role has been underestimated.

questions.q: It explains the extinction as the result of events lasting hundreds of thousands of years.
questions.evidence: Over hundreds of thousands of years, these eruptions produced vast floods of lava.
questions.explanation: Gradual decline (A) describes "millions of years" of climate and sea-level change, not events lasting "hundreds of thousands of years". C is used twice.

questions.q: It is favoured by many scientists today, with one cause regarded as the main trigger.
questions.evidence: Many scientists now favour a combined explanation, in which the asteroid was the main trigger.

lesson.title: Hard Matching Features — shifting positions and cross-references
lesson.text:
In Hard sets:

researchers may appear in several paragraphs, sometimes responding to each other; a researcher may revise an earlier view, or collaborate with a former opponent; statements are heavily paraphrased and may describe a method, a conclusion or a response;

some features may be unused.

For each feature, collect every mention before answering, and note the sequence (original claim → challenge → response).

questions.q: found that the link between income and satisfaction was similar at all income levels when measured proportionally
questions.evidence: a doubling of income was associated with a similar increase in satisfaction whether a person or country started rich or poor.

questions.q: suggested that rising expectations might cancel out the effect of increased wealth
questions.evidence: when everyone becomes richer, and expectations rise accordingly, people feel no better off.
questions.explanation: This is Easterlin's explanation of the paradox.

questions.q: used a method that recorded feelings at the moment they were experienced
questions.evidence: a smartphone application that asked people at random moments how they were feeling.
questions.explanation: This records feelings as they happen.

questions.q: acted as an impartial participant in a joint re-examination of data
questions.evidence: with the psychologist Barbara Mellers acting as a neutral mediator.

questions.q: separated the way people judge their lives from their everyday emotions
questions.evidence: distinguished between two aspects of well-being: people's overall evaluation of their lives, and their day-to-day emotional experience.
questions.explanation: The distinction is introduced in the paragraph on Kahneman and Deaton's study, which applied it.

questions.q: argued that an opposing study relied on temporary changes
questions.evidence: Easterlin responded that their findings relied on short-term fluctuations.
questions.explanation: Easterlin's response appears in paragraph C, the Stevenson–Wolfers paragraph, so you must track his later mention. A is used twice.

questions.q: found that a subgroup of people did not become happier above a certain income
questions.evidence: for the least happy group ... happiness stopped increasing above a certain income.
questions.explanation: This is the joint finding. C found a plateau for emotional well-being in general, not for a subgroup, which makes C a trap.

questions.q: claimed that recall-based survey questions were less direct than their own approach
questions.evidence: His method ... measured feelings more directly than survey questions asking people to remember how they had felt the previous day.

lesson.title: Scholars who qualify one another
lesson.text: Hard passages about academic debates may present scholars who build on, qualify or reject one another's work. The same topic, such as "the stability of printed texts", may be discussed by two scholars who take opposite positions. Statements will describe a position precisely. Read each scholar's section and note their distinctive claim, then check statements against that claim.

questions.q: argued that confidence in printed texts developed through social arrangements rather than being inherent in the technology
questions.evidence: The reliability ... was not a natural feature of printing but had to be established gradually through social practices.

questions.q: focused on the financial and practical organisation of book production
questions.evidence: they examined the book as a commercial product: how printing businesses were financed, how paper was supplied.

questions.q: linked printing to major religious and scientific changes
questions.evidence: Eisenstein connected these changes to major developments including the Protestant Reformation and the Scientific Revolution.

questions.q: proposed that printing altered patterns of thinking
questions.evidence: printing did not merely spread information more widely but changed the way people thought.
questions.explanation: "Changed the way people thought" = "altered patterns of thinking".

questions.q: highlighted the importance of inexpensive, short publications
questions.evidence: short, cheap items: pamphlets, notices, calendars and news sheets.

questions.q: was criticised for making claims without sufficient evidence
questions.evidence: many historians regarded them as speculative and supported by little systematic evidence.

questions.q: pointed out that many early printers were commercially unsuccessful
questions.evidence: many early printing businesses failed.
questions.explanation: Febvre and Martin (B) describe printers as profit-seeking, but only Pettegree notes their frequent failure. E is used twice.

questions.q: argued that identical copies allowed scholars to build on each other's work
questions.evidence: Printed texts could be reproduced in identical copies, allowing scholars ... to build on one another's work.
questions.explanation: Johns (D) disputes this, which makes D a trap. C is used twice.

lesson.title: Features that are explanations, not people
lesson.text: When the features are hypotheses rather than named scholars, the passage may describe each one through the words of several researchers, and may present evidence for one hypothesis in a paragraph mainly about another. Map each statement to the explanation it concerns, not to the paragraph in which it appears.

questions.q: Its supporters cite natural records preserved in lakes and caves.
questions.evidence: analysed layers of sediment at the bottom of lakes ... as well as mineral deposits in caves.

questions.q: It is questioned because a similar factor had existed for centuries without causing collapse.
questions.evidence: although warfare had been common throughout Maya history without causing collapse.
questions.explanation: This is the objection to the warfare explanation.

questions.q: It suggests that rulers lost support when they failed to guarantee good conditions.
questions.evidence: If kings failed to deliver prosperity ... their authority may have been undermined.
questions.explanation: Drought appears here only as an example, so A is a trap. The statement concerns the political mechanism.

questions.q: It proposes that one cause may have worsened another by affecting rainfall.
questions.evidence: deforestation may also have made droughts worse, since forests help to maintain local rainfall.
questions.explanation: This appears in the environmental-damage paragraph. The claim that deforestation worsens drought belongs to that explanation.

questions.q: It is said to account best for the differences in timing between cities.
questions.evidence: it fits the varied timing and pattern of abandonment better than any one factor alone.

questions.q: It is challenged by the fact that some drier places lasted longer.
questions.evidence: some cities in drier areas survived longer than those in wetter ones.

questions.q: It notes a change in the geography of trade.
questions.evidence: trade routes appear to have shifted from inland rivers towards coastal sea routes.

questions.q: Some researchers doubt it because the Maya were skilled at managing their land.
questions.evidence: Others caution that the Maya had sophisticated methods of managing land.

lesson.title: Strong and weak versions of an idea
lesson.text: Debates often distinguish a strong version of a theory (language determines thought) from a weak version (language influences thought in some areas). Scholars may reject the strong version but accept the weak one. Statements may describe either. Check carefully which version each scholar supports, rejects or provides evidence for.

questions.q: argued that languages differ mainly in what they require speakers to express
questions.evidence: they differ in what they oblige speakers to express.

questions.q: made a claim about a particular language that later research contradicted
questions.evidence: Later researchers ... found that it does, in fact, contain many expressions of time, and Whorf's specific claims ... have been widely rejected.
questions.explanation: Whorf's claim about Hopi was contradicted.

questions.q: found that the order in which languages acquire certain words is largely predictable
questions.evidence: further terms were added in a largely predictable order.

questions.q: pointed to thinking in beings who have no language
questions.evidence: pointed out that babies and animals are capable of complex thought without language.

questions.q: studied people whose language describes location using fixed geographical directions
questions.evidence: speakers of Kuuk Thaayorre ... uses compass directions.

questions.q: argued that a physical feature shared by all humans limits variation between languages
questions.evidence: colour naming is constrained by universal features of human vision.
questions.explanation: "Human vision" is the shared physical feature. B is used twice.

questions.q: denied that languages make certain thoughts impossible
questions.evidence: Languages, he argues, do not prevent their speakers from thinking particular thoughts.
questions.explanation: Pinker (C) also opposes strong claims, but this specific formulation belongs to Deutscher. E is used twice.

questions.q: used a strongly worded dismissal of an extreme version of a theory
questions.evidence: Pinker described the strong version of Whorf's hypothesis as 'wrong, all wrong'.

lesson.title: Features that are measures or indices
lesson.text: When features are measures (indices, indicators, systems), statements describe what each one includes, excludes, was designed for, or has been criticised for. Several measures may include similar components (for example, health), so look for the precise combination or the specific criticism.

questions.q: It subtracts the cost of social and environmental problems.
questions.evidence: while subtracting costs such as crime, pollution, the loss of natural resources and inequality.

questions.q: It can reveal differences between countries with similar incomes.
questions.evidence: Countries with similar incomes can rank very differently on the HDI.

questions.q: One of its developers warned against using it to judge welfare.
questions.evidence: Simon Kuznets ... warned that the welfare of a nation could scarcely be inferred from a measure of national income.

questions.q: It did not propose one alternative but several indicators.
questions.evidence: did not propose a single replacement. Instead, it recommended ... a range of indicators.

questions.q: It relies on detailed surveys of many aspects of life to guide government decisions.
questions.evidence: measures well-being through detailed surveys ... and uses the results to guide policy.

questions.q: Its critics question the way its components have been selected and combined.
questions.evidence: the choice of components and the way they are combined are somewhat arbitrary.
questions.explanation: The GPI (C) is criticised for assigning money values, which is a different criticism and makes C a trap. B is used twice.

questions.q: It treats spending on repairing damage as a positive contribution.
questions.evidence: GDP counts spending on activities that may reflect harm ... the costs of repairing damage after a disaster.

questions.q: It has shown slower growth than conventional economic measures in several countries.
questions.evidence: the GPI has grown much more slowly than GDP since the 1970s.

lesson.title: Final review — the complete method

questions.q: It was supported by an experiment comparing two species on machines.
questions.evidence: measured the energy used by chimpanzees and humans walking on treadmills.

questions.q: It links upright walking to relationships between males and females.
questions.evidence: associated with the formation of pair bonds between males and females.

questions.q: It assumed that shrinking forests had been replaced by open grassland.
questions.evidence: climate change in Africa caused forests to shrink and open grasslands to expand.
questions.explanation: This is the starting assumption of the savanna hypothesis, which later woodland evidence (Paragraph C) challenged.

questions.q: It may have become more relevant at a later stage than when walking began.
questions.evidence: the importance of this advantage for the origin ... has been questioned, although it may have become more significant later.

questions.q: It suggests that individual variation within a species could be acted on by selection.
questions.evidence: some individuals walked on two legs more efficiently than others, suggesting that natural selection could have acted on such variation.

questions.q: It is criticised for depending on untestable claims about behaviour.
questions.evidence: it makes assumptions about social behaviour that are difficult to test.

questions.q: It proposed that upright posture helped individuals see over vegetation.
questions.evidence: to see over tall grass to spot predators and food.

questions.q: It is supported by the view that early species both walked upright and climbed.
questions.evidence: early species combining upright walking with climbing.
questions.explanation: This is the combined, gradual view.

lesson.title: Predict before you look
lesson.text: In easy sets, each beginning points clearly to one sentence in the passage. Find that sentence and predict the ending in your own words, for example "...because the army needed food that would last". Then find the ending that expresses your prediction. This prevents you from being attracted by endings that simply repeat passage vocabulary.

questions.q: The French government offered a prize because
questions.evidence: offered a large prize to anyone who could develop a better method of preserving food for its forces.

questions.q: Appert thought that his method worked because
questions.evidence: He believed that the key was to keep air away from the food.
questions.explanation: This is Appert's own belief. A is Pasteur's explanation, which makes A a trap for this beginning.

questions.q: Pasteur later explained that food goes bad because
questions.evidence: food spoils because of the growth of microorganisms.

questions.q: Tin cans were more practical than glass bottles because
questions.evidence: Tin cans were stronger and lighter than glass.

questions.q: Canned food became available to ordinary people because
questions.evidence: machines were developed that could make cans much more quickly and cheaply.
questions.explanation: H is a trap: the can opener is mentioned, but it is not the reason canned food reached ordinary households.

lesson.title: Cause, effect and purpose endings
lesson.text: Many beginnings contain because, so that, as a result, or verbs such as help, reduce or lead to. Decide whether the beginning needs a cause, an effect or a purpose, then look for endings of that type. An ending can be true but of the wrong type, for example a cause when the beginning needs a result.

questions.q: In the past, many wetlands were drained because
questions.evidence: they were widely regarded as useless or unhealthy land ... As a result, many were drained.

questions.q: Draining wetlands can make floods worse because
questions.evidence: When wetlands are drained, water runs off the land more quickly.
questions.explanation: The beginning needs a cause, and "runs off more quickly" = "flows off more rapidly".

questions.q: Some towns have built artificial wetlands
questions.evidence: created artificial wetlands to treat wastewater as a cheaper alternative.
questions.explanation: The beginning needs a purpose. H is also grammatically possible, but the passage does not say artificial wetlands were built for fish.

questions.q: Draining peatlands contributes to climate change because
questions.evidence: the peat dries out and begins to decompose, releasing carbon dioxide.
questions.explanation: G is true of peatlands but does not explain why draining them contributes to climate change, so G is a true-but-unrelated trap.

questions.q: Restoring wetlands often involves
questions.evidence: Restoration projects have blocked drainage channels, allowing water levels to rise again.

lesson.title: Beginnings with time words
lesson.text: Beginnings often include time references: "In ancient times,", "After the 1820s,", "Today,". These tell you exactly where to look in the passage. Endings from a different period may be true statements but describe the wrong time, which is a common trap.

questions.q: In the centuries after the ancient period, much of the light from lighthouses was wasted because
questions.evidence: it shone in all directions, including upwards and towards the land.

questions.q: Fresnel's lens was more effective than earlier designs because
questions.evidence: almost all of it was directed into a strong, narrow beam.
questions.explanation: E contradicts the passage: the lens was not a single piece of glass.

questions.q: Different lighthouses used different patterns of light so that
questions.evidence: To help sailors identify particular lighthouses ... allowing them to work out their position.

questions.q: Lighthouse keepers were sometimes isolated for long periods because
questions.evidence: located on isolated rocks or islands, where keepers could be cut off ... during storms.
questions.explanation: G is a keyword trap: fog is mentioned in a different context.

questions.q: Some lighthouses remain in use today because
questions.evidence: continue to operate as a reliable backup.
questions.explanation: "Reliable backup" = "dependable alternative". H is not stated.

lesson.title: Name and invention beginnings
lesson.text: When a beginning names an inventor or product ("Cristofori's instrument..."), the ending often describes what was new about it or why it succeeded. Look for the sentence that explains the innovation's significance, not just its existence.

questions.q: Harpsichord players could not vary volume because
questions.evidence: Pressing a key harder or more gently makes almost no difference.

questions.q: Cristofori's instrument allowed players to control volume because
questions.evidence: The harder the player pressed a key, the faster the hammer moved and the louder the note.
questions.explanation: G is a false detail: the hammers were covered in leather, and the strings were struck, not plucked.

questions.q: Iron frames were introduced so that
questions.evidence: cast-iron frames, which could withstand the enormous tension of thicker, tighter strings ... much louder and richer sound.
questions.explanation: F gives the demand behind the change, but it does not fit the purpose structure "so that".

questions.q: Upright pianos became popular in homes because
questions.evidence: took up less space than large grand pianos and were cheaper to produce.

questions.q: Digital pianos attract some buyers because
questions.evidence: do not need tuning.
questions.explanation: H refers to acoustic pianos, not digital ones.

lesson.title: Scientific uncertainty in endings
lesson.text: Science passages often say that effects are not yet fully understood. An ending that states an effect as certain may not match a beginning about what scientists know. Match the level of certainty: if the beginning says "Researchers are still unsure...", the ending must express uncertainty or an unanswered question.

questions.q: Plastic breaks into smaller pieces rather than biodegrading because
questions.evidence: plastic does not biodegrade in the way that natural materials do. Instead, it gradually breaks into smaller ... pieces.

questions.q: Washing synthetic clothes contributes to microplastic pollution because
questions.evidence: sheds tiny fibres every time it is washed, and many of these pass through wastewater treatment plants into rivers and the sea.

questions.q: Scientists are not yet sure whether
questions.evidence: Researchers are uncertain, however, whether the concentrations found in the natural environment are high enough to cause significant harm.
questions.explanation: D and H are known facts, not uncertainties, which breaks the "not yet sure" pattern.

questions.q: Removing microplastics from nature is not considered realistic because
questions.evidence: Because microplastics are so small and so widespread, removing them ... is practically impossible.

questions.q: Improved wastewater treatment does not fully solve the problem because
questions.evidence: the captured particles then end up in sewage sludge, which is often spread on farmland.

lesson.title: Checking grammar as a second filter

questions.q: During the world wars, governments encouraged people to grow vegetables in order to
questions.evidence: to reduce pressure on food supplies.
questions.explanation: After "in order to", only endings beginning with a base verb fit: A, D or G. Only D matches the wartime purpose. G is from the 1970s revival, which makes it a wrong-period trap.

questions.q: Many wartime gardens were abandoned because
questions.evidence: many were abandoned as food became more plentiful.
questions.explanation: "More plentiful" = "easier to obtain". B describes closure because of construction, which the passage links only to modern gardens (Paragraph F).

questions.q: Some gardens use raised beds because
questions.evidence: soil contaminated by previous industrial use must be ... replaced with raised beds.

questions.q: Schools use community gardens in order to
questions.evidence: Schools use them to teach children where food comes from.

questions.q: Some gardens close after years of work because
questions.evidence: when the owner decides to build on it, the garden may have to close, even after years of work.

lesson.title: Several endings on the same topic
lesson.text: At Medium level, three or four endings may all relate to the same animal or idea, differing in a key detail (method vs result, cause vs effect, one species vs another). Identify the specific relationship the beginning requires, then choose the ending that expresses that relationship for the correct subject.

questions.q: Naked mole-rats are unusual among rodents because
questions.evidence: their risk of dying does not appear to increase significantly as they grow older.

questions.q: The age of Greenland sharks was estimated by examining
questions.evidence: analysed the lenses of the sharks' eyes, which contain proteins formed before birth that do not change afterwards.
questions.explanation: H is explicitly ruled out: "cannot be estimated from growth rings".

questions.q: Greenland shark populations are at particular risk because
questions.evidence: Females are thought not to reach maturity until they are well over a hundred years old ... populations take so long to replace individuals.
questions.explanation: F is true of the shark, but the passage links cold water to their long life, not to their vulnerability. This is a same-subject trap.

questions.q: Scientists were prompted to investigate the age of bowhead whales because
questions.evidence: harpoon points ... of a type used by local hunters before the late nineteenth century, were found embedded.
questions.explanation: I is not stated as the prompt.

questions.q: Bowhead whales may be protected from cancer because
questions.evidence: changes in genes involved in repairing DNA and controlling cell division, which may help the whales avoid cancer.

questions.q: Researchers warn against expecting quick human benefits because
questions.evidence: findings in other species may not transfer directly to humans.

title: The Price Is Not Always Right

lesson.title: Endings that reverse cause and effect
lesson.text: A strong Medium distractor uses the right ideas but in the wrong direction. For example, the passage says "prices rise as seats fill", and the ending says "seats fill because prices rise". Before choosing, check which idea is the cause and which is the effect in the passage, and make sure the complete sentence keeps that order.

questions.q: Airlines developed revenue management after
questions.evidence: after government controls on air fares were removed and competition increased.

questions.q: Unsold airline seats are particularly costly because
questions.evidence: once a flight has departed, an empty seat can never be sold, so its potential revenue is lost for ever.

questions.q: Restrictions on cheap tickets are designed to
questions.evidence: restrictions ... which make them less attractive to business travellers.
questions.explanation: I reverses the facts: business travellers book at short notice, not early.

questions.q: Cheaper seats may be made available again when
questions.evidence: If bookings are slower than expected, cheaper seats may be released again.

questions.q: Supporters claim that higher business fares
questions.evidence: Because business travellers pay higher fares, airlines can offer cheap seats to price-sensitive travellers.
questions.explanation: G reverses the critics' point, since complexity makes comparison harder.

questions.q: Prices often change between searches because
questions.evidence: Prices often change ... because seats in a cheaper fare class have been sold or because the airline's system has updated its prices.
questions.explanation: E is the popular belief that the passage says has "little evidence", so it is the cause-reversal trap.

lesson.title: Claims, evidence and criticism in one passage
lesson.text: When a passage presents a theory, its supporting evidence and later criticism, beginnings may refer to any of these three. Check whether a beginning asks about what the theory claims, what evidence was used or what critics found. Endings from the wrong category are the main distractors.

questions.q: Dunbar's original idea was based on the observation that
questions.evidence: group size was related to the size of the neocortex ... relative to the rest of the brain.
questions.explanation: I is a true detail, but it is not the observation that his idea was based on.

questions.q: Dunbar suggested that language developed partly because
questions.evidence: as human groups became too large for grooming to maintain, language evolved partly as a more efficient form of 'vocal grooming'.

questions.q: Research on social media suggests that
questions.evidence: the number with whom they interact regularly and meaningfully is much smaller.
questions.explanation: E is not supported, and it contradicts the finding.

questions.q: The 2021 reanalysis concluded that
questions.evidence: They concluded that the data could not support any precise figure.

questions.q: Some critics suggest that the primate relationship may be explained by
questions.evidence: may reflect factors other than social demands, such as diet.

questions.q: Even Dunbar's critics tend to accept that
questions.evidence: even critics generally accept that there are limits ... since relationships require time and attention.
questions.explanation: C refers only to online contacts and is not the general point that critics accept, which makes it a same-topic trap.

lesson.title: Benefits and conflicts
lesson.text: Conservation passages often balance benefits (ecological, economic) against conflicts (with farmers or landowners). Beginnings may begin neutrally ("Beaver dams...") and require you to choose between a positive and a negative ending. Check the specific sentence the beginning refers to. Both kinds of ending may be true somewhere in the passage.

questions.q: Beavers disappeared from Britain because
questions.evidence: hunted to extinction ... prized for its fur, its meat and a substance from its glands.

questions.q: The Devon population was allowed to remain because
questions.evidence: Rather than removing a population discovered on a river in Devon, the authorities allowed a five-year monitored trial.
questions.explanation: I describes how the beavers may have arrived, not why they were allowed to stay.

questions.q: Beaver dams may reduce flooding downstream because
questions.evidence: water is held back and released gradually.

questions.q: Concerns that dams would block the movement of fish
questions.evidence: research suggests that fish are often able to pass dams ... and that the ponds can provide valuable habitat.
questions.explanation: "Partly eased" matches the research reducing the concern without removing it. F is contradicted, since releases have begun.

questions.q: Pipes can be fitted through dams in order to
questions.evidence: Pipes can be installed through dams to limit the height of the water.

questions.q: The return of the beaver is seen as a test of
questions.evidence: a test of whether a society can accept a native species that changes the landscape in ways that are sometimes inconvenient.

lesson.title: Beginnings that refer to consequences of events
lesson.text: History passages link events to their results: "The First World War led governments to...", "The 1920 conference resulted in...". Several endings may describe changes in the same area, such as passport design, from different periods. Match the specific event to its specific consequence, using the paragraph where the event appears.

questions.q: Medieval letters of safe conduct were mainly intended to
questions.evidence: requesting that they be allowed to pass freely and protected ... more as a request for protection than as proof of identity or nationality.

questions.q: Passport requirements were relaxed in the nineteenth century because
questions.evidence: checking the documents of large numbers of passengers proved impractical.

questions.q: The First World War led governments to
questions.evidence: Governments, concerned about spies ... introduced strict requirements for travellers to carry passports.

questions.q: The 1920 conference resulted in
questions.evidence: agreed on common guidelines, recommending a standard booklet format with a photograph.
questions.explanation: F belongs to a later period, and only "in some cases", so it is a wrong-period trap.

questions.q: Machine-readable zones were introduced in order to
questions.evidence: could be read automatically by scanners ... speeding up checks.
questions.explanation: H refers to electronic chips, a later development.

questions.q: Some commentators observe that freedom of travel depends largely on
questions.evidence: nationality, which is usually determined by where they happen to be born.

lesson.title: Examples that illustrate a general point
lesson.text: Some beginnings name a specific example ("Blackbirds in cities..."), and the correct ending states what that example shows or how the animal has changed. Other endings may describe other animals' adaptations. Track which example belongs to which change, and don't be distracted by endings that are correct for a different species.

questions.q: Birds in noisy areas sing at a higher pitch because
questions.evidence: higher notes are less masked by the low rumble of traffic.
questions.explanation: I explains why some birds sing earlier, not why they sing at a higher pitch.

questions.q: Urban animals tend to be bolder because
questions.evidence: in environments where humans are everywhere but rarely dangerous.

questions.q: Peregrine falcons have benefited from cities because
questions.evidence: adopted tall buildings ... as substitute cliffs. Cities also provide an abundant supply of prey.

questions.q: Raising lizards in identical conditions indicated that
questions.evidence: the offspring of city lizards still showed these features, suggesting that the differences were inherited.
questions.explanation: H is the opposite conclusion, that the differences come from how the lizards develop.

questions.q: Moths from polluted areas may be less useful to plants because
questions.evidence: moths that fly less may be less effective as pollinators.

questions.q: Researchers regard cities as valuable for scientific study because
questions.evidence: natural laboratories in which evolution can be observed over relatively short periods of time.
questions.explanation: G describes which species thrive, not why cities are useful for study.

title: Four Days' Work, Five Days' Pay?

lesson.title: Findings vs limitations
lesson.text: Research passages often report findings and then limitations ("however, the companies taking part were not typical..."). Beginnings may ask about either. Look for signal words that introduce limitations (however, critics note, one weakness, it is unclear whether). The ending must match the category the beginning requires.

questions.q: Supporters argue that productivity need not fall because
questions.evidence: if unnecessary meetings and distractions are cut.

questions.q: Companies in the UK trial were allowed to
questions.evidence: They were free to design their own arrangements.
questions.explanation: G is contradicted by "maintaining full pay".

questions.q: Most participating companies decided at the end of the trial to
questions.evidence: the great majority of participating companies said that they would continue with the four-day week.

questions.q: In some organisations, the shorter week led to
questions.evidence: the pressure to complete the same work in less time increased stress on working days.
questions.explanation: This is a finding about some organisations.

questions.q: The results may not apply to all businesses because
questions.evidence: The companies that took part volunteered ... Many were relatively small organisations in areas such as marketing.
questions.explanation: This is a limitation. I is not stated, since manufacturing results are unknown.

questions.q: Critics also suggest that the trial's length means
questions.evidence: a six-month trial may not reveal longer-term effects.

lesson.title: Technical explanations in endings
lesson.text: Science passages may explain a mechanism in several steps. Endings may describe the mechanism, its effect or a practical application. Some distractors misstate the mechanism in a way that sounds plausible, for example "pigments reflect blue light" when the passage says there is no blue pigment. Check the passage's exact explanation.

questions.q: Morpho butterflies appear blue because
questions.evidence: reflections from different layers interfere ... blue light waves reinforce each other.
questions.explanation: C directly contradicts "contain no blue pigment".

questions.q: Filling the spaces in a morpho wing with liquid shows that
questions.evidence: the blue colour disappears, showing that it depends on the structure rather than any chemical.

questions.q: Structural colours often seem to change when an observer moves because
questions.evidence: Because the colour depends on the angle from which light is reflected ... appear to change as the observer moves.
questions.explanation: H is a keyword trap: melanin is present, but it does not explain the changing appearance.

questions.q: Pigment-based colours in old museum specimens often fade because
questions.evidence: Because they [structural colours] do not depend on chemicals that can break down in sunlight, they can remain bright ... whereas pigment-based colours in other specimens have faded.
questions.explanation: The contrast shows that pigments fade because their chemicals break down. A describes structural colour, not pigment, so it does not complete this beginning.

questions.q: Structural colours are attractive for banknotes because
questions.evidence: Structural colours are also difficult to copy precisely, which makes them attractive for security features on banknotes.
questions.explanation: I is contradicted by "reproducing them on a large scale at low cost remains a challenge".

questions.q: Researchers are studying disordered structures because
questions.evidence: disordered structures ... produce colours that look the same from all angles.

lesson.title: Hard Matching Sentence Endings — abstract endings

questions.q: Lancaster's use of lemon juice did not lead to wider adoption because
questions.evidence: Yet the practice was not adopted systematically.
questions.explanation: "Systematically" = "in a consistent, organised way". J is not stated.

questions.q: The effectiveness of the treatment Lind later recommended was reduced by
questions.evidence: methods of preserving juice by heating it, which destroyed much of its effectiveness.
questions.explanation: "Heating" = "a processing method", and "destroyed much of its effectiveness" = "damaged the active substance". G is a keyword trap about a later discovery.

questions.q: Rogers argued that innovations spread faster when
questions.evidence: when their results are visible to others.
questions.explanation: H reverses Rogers' point: innovations promoted by outsiders may meet resistance (Paragraph E).

questions.q: According to Rogers, an innovation may meet resistance if
questions.evidence: one that seems to challenge the status or expertise of established professionals, may meet resistance.

questions.q: Some effective health measures spread slowly because
questions.evidence: they required changes in behaviour, conflicted with local beliefs about illness.

questions.q: The writer's main conclusion is that the adoption of innovations depends on
questions.evidence: evidence alone is rarely sufficient ... can matter as much as how well it works.
questions.explanation: I contradicts Paragraph E ("can be more influential than scientific evidence").

lesson.title: Paradoxes and counter-intuitive reasoning
lesson.text: Some Hard passages explain a paradox. Here, a medicine that is extremely valuable to society earns little money. Beginnings may ask about the paradox's cause or about the proposed solution. Endings may be deliberately common-sense statements that the passage rejects. Follow the passage's reasoning step by step, even when it seems surprising.

questions.q: Resistance develops because the use of antibiotics
questions.evidence: Whenever antibiotics are used, bacteria that happen to be resistant survive and multiply.

questions.q: New antibiotics generate relatively little income because
questions.evidence: doctors keep them in reserve for patients with infections that do not respond to older drugs.
questions.explanation: F describes drugs for long-term conditions, the opposite case. H is the common-sense misreading that the passage rejects ("used as little as possible").

questions.q: Discovering new antibiotics has become harder partly because
questions.evidence: The easiest antibiotics to discover ... were identified decades ago.
questions.explanation: "Easiest to discover" = "most accessible sources ... already exploited".

questions.q: Economists argue that "pull" incentives are needed because
questions.evidence: because the main problem is the lack of revenue after approval rather than only the cost of research.
questions.explanation: I overstates the argument: push incentives are not said to be unnecessary; pull incentives are "also needed".

questions.q: The UK scheme is designed so that
questions.evidence: separates a company's income from the quantity of antibiotics sold.

questions.q: Experts believe that new payment schemes require international cooperation because
questions.evidence: since the global market for any single antibiotic is shared.
questions.explanation: J is true, but it relates to reducing use, not to payment schemes, so it is a true-but-unrelated trap.

lesson.title: Popularised versions vs original research
lesson.text: Hard passages may distinguish between what research actually found and how it was popularised. Beginnings may concern either. An ending that reflects the popular version may be correct for a beginning about popular belief but wrong for a beginning about the original study. Identify whose claim each beginning concerns.

questions.q: In the 1993 study, the most accomplished students differed from the others in that
questions.evidence: the best students had, on average, accumulated considerably more hours of practice.
questions.explanation: H reflects the traditional "talent" view, which the study did not report.

questions.q: According to Ericsson, relatively few people reach the highest levels because
questions.evidence: Deliberate practice ... is demanding and often not enjoyable, which is why relatively few people sustain it.

questions.q: Ericsson objected to the "ten-thousand-hour rule" partly because
questions.evidence: ten thousand hours was simply an approximate average for one group of violinists ... the number of hours needed varied greatly.
questions.explanation: J is false, because the study was of violinists.

questions.q: The 2014 analysis found that practice
questions.evidence: a substantial part in games such as chess, but much less in fields such as professions and education.

questions.q: Ericsson's supporters challenged the 2014 findings on the grounds that
questions.evidence: many of the studies included did not measure deliberate practice accurately.

questions.q: The writer suggests that coaches should
questions.evidence: teachers and coaches should focus on the quality of practice rather than simply its quantity.
questions.explanation: I is the opposite of the writer's advice, and G is the popular claim the writer calls "exaggerated".

lesson.title: Failures that led to later success
lesson.text: History-of-science passages often describe an early attempt that failed, but whose method was later vindicated. Beginnings may ask why it failed or what it demonstrated. These need different endings: one about the obstacle, one about the lasting value. Don't confuse them.

questions.q: FitzRoy's forecasts were made possible by
questions.evidence: Scientific forecasting became possible only when observations from distant places could be gathered quickly ... the electric telegraph.

questions.q: After FitzRoy's death, storm warnings were quickly reintroduced because
questions.evidence: storm warnings to shipping, which fishermen and sailors had found valuable, were soon restored.

questions.q: Richardson's forecast failed partly because
questions.evidence: errors in the initial data and ... features of his calculations that amplified small errors.
questions.explanation: H explains why the method was slow, not why the forecast was wrong. This is the failure-versus-vindication distinction from the lesson.

questions.q: Despite its failure, Richardson's work was significant because
questions.evidence: His basic approach, however, was sound.
questions.explanation: This is the lasting value of his work.

questions.q: Lorenz concluded that detailed long-range forecasts are impossible because
questions.evidence: tiny differences in the starting values ... eventually produced completely different forecasts.
questions.explanation: F contradicts the passage, since the equations were known and used.

questions.q: Ensemble forecasting allows forecasters to
questions.evidence: this uncertainty can be expressed as a probability.
questions.explanation: J is too strong, because ensembles measure uncertainty but do not remove it.

lesson.title: Refutations
lesson.text: When a passage presents a famous theory and then evidence that refutes or limits it, beginnings may concern the original claim, the counter-evidence or the refined conclusion. Endings may restate the original theory's prediction; these complete beginnings about the theory, not beginnings about the evidence. Map each beginning to its stage.

questions.q: In Hardin's example, each herder continues adding animals because
questions.evidence: Each herder gains the full benefit of adding an extra animal ... but bears only a small share of the cost.
questions.explanation: F is Hardin's conclusion, not the reason for each herder's behaviour.

questions.q: Some policies based on Hardin's ideas led to greater exploitation because
questions.evidence: traditional community rules had been removed but nothing effective had replaced them.

questions.q: Ostrom's fieldwork showed that shared resources could be managed sustainably when
questions.evidence: The users themselves had developed rules governing who could use the resource ... and how rules were enforced.

questions.q: In successful cases studied by Ostrom, people who repeatedly broke the rules
questions.evidence: penalties that increased with repeated offences.

questions.q: Ostrom argued that Hardin's model was flawed because it assumed that
questions.evidence: Hardin's model rested on an assumption ... that users could not communicate or make agreements with one another.

questions.q: Applying Ostrom's findings to global resources is difficult because
questions.evidence: enormous numbers of users ... who do not share a community.

lesson.title: Final review — the complete method
lesson.text:
This final set combines the main skills: abstract endings, several true-but-unrelated endings, reversed cause and effect, and beginnings that require you to combine information. For each beginning:

1. Locate the passage section.

2. Predict the ending in plain words.

3. Match your prediction to the abstract ending.

4. Confirm meaning, scope and grammar.

questions.q: Towns grew up at portage sites because
questions.evidence: places where boats ... had to be unloaded and their cargo carried overland.
questions.explanation: G explains the towns' loss of purpose, not their origin, so it is a cause-reversal trap.

questions.q: Cities can continue to grow after their original advantages disappear because
questions.evidence: Businesses locate there because other businesses and workers are already present; workers move there because jobs are available.

questions.q: The Roman roads study suggests that historical advantages last only when
questions.evidence: historical advantages persist only if they continue to be used.

questions.q: The recovery of bombed cities indicates that
questions.evidence: the advantages of a city's location and its economic networks can survive even the destruction of much of its physical fabric.

questions.q: Path dependence may be harmful when
questions.evidence: Some cities are located in places that are increasingly vulnerable ... the same forces that keep them in place may make adaptation ... more difficult.

questions.q: New cities in places without existing advantages often
questions.evidence: Efforts to create entirely new cities in locations without existing advantages often struggle to attract people and businesses.
